name: Calorie deficit / calorie counting

lead: A calorie deficit means eating less energy than you burn, and calorie counting is tracking intake to keep that gap. It is the usual foundation of a cut in looksmaxxing circles, used to strip body fat and reveal jawline, cheekbones and abs.

When intake is below energy expenditure, the body draws on stored energy, mostly fat but also some lean tissue. Calorie restriction is well established to produce weight and fat loss. The intake best for health is not known, and there is little research on appearance outcomes specifically.

paras: People estimate maintenance calories, set a daily target below it, and log food with an app or scale, usually alongside resistance training and higher protein to hold muscle. Visible changes build over weeks to months.

Reported effects include cold sensitivity, hormonal and menstrual changes, and, in severe restriction as in the Minnesota experiment, muscle wasting, anemia and depression. Moderate restriction may be harmful for people who are already lean.

angle.text: A calorie deficit tracked by counting is the baseline method in looksmaxxing circles for cutting body fat to reveal jawline, cheekbones and abs. Fat loss from a deficit is well established, while research on facial appearance specifically is limited.

lead: A calorie deficit means eating less energy than the body uses, and calorie counting is the practice of tracking food intake, usually with an app or scale, to maintain that gap. In looksmaxxing communities it is the baseline method for losing body fat to reveal facial and body definition, often called "cutting."

Calorie restriction, the research term, is defined as reducing energy intake below energy requirements without causing malnutrition. Wikipedia notes that it causes weight and fat loss, while the calorie intake and fat mass best for human health are not known.[1] US dietary guidelines and scientific societies recommend calorie control for people with overweight.[1]
infobox: Fat loss for leaner face and physique

paras: A deficit is created by eating less, moving more, or both. Practitioners estimate maintenance intake, then set a target below it and weigh and log foods. Forum participants discuss deficit size, protein targets and refeeds in this context.

Guidelines cited by Wikipedia suggest weight-loss goals of 7 to 10 percent for prediabetes and 5 to 15 percent for diabetes, combined with exercise, and note that weight loss may be followed by gradual regain of 1 to 2 kg per year.[1]

Reducing intake by 20 to 30 percent while meeting nutrient needs was associated with an average loss of 7.9 kg in the studies summarized there. Moderate restriction may be harmful for lean people with low body fat.[1]

The Minnesota Starvation Experiment, in which 32 lean young men ate about 40 percent less for six months, produced about 25 percent body weight loss, with 67 percent from fat mass and 17 percent from fat-free mass; participants developed anemia, edema, muscle wasting, weakness, dizziness and depression. The diet was nutritionally inadequate and is not representative of a designed calorie-restricted diet.[1]

Human and animal calorie-restriction studies exist, but no studies were found that test calorie counting specifically for facial appearance. Rhesus macaque studies reached different conclusions on lifespan: the Wisconsin study reported increased lifespan, while the National Institute on Aging study did not in non-obese monkeys.[1]

Wikipedia lists cold sensitivity, menstrual irregularities, infertility and hormonal changes as possible effects during weight loss.[1] Calorie tracking is also discussed in clinical literature in relation to eating disorders, though that was not covered in the sources reviewed here.

lore.intro: Calorie deficits are treated in forums as the foundation of cutting, with debates about how large the deficit should be.

claims.claim: A modest deficit loses fat while keeping muscle and hair, whereas extreme deficits harm both.

timeline.event: Minnesota Starvation Experiment studies semi-starvation in 32 lean men.[1]
Wisconsin and NIA rhesus macaque calorie-restriction studies begin.[1]
